analysis.body:
# Government AI Adoption and Implementation

Federal agencies are in the early stages of deploying artificial intelligence, with significant gaps in coordination and risk management. According to GAO audits, twenty of twenty-three agencies reported about 1,200 current and planned artificial intelligence use cases, while three agencies reported not having uses for AI. These use cases span analyzing data from cameras and radar to identify border activities, analyzing photographs from drones, and targeting of scientific specimens for planetary rovers. NASA and the Department of Commerce reported the highest number of AI use cases. However, most of these reported AI use cases were in the planning phase and not yet in production; in about 200 instances, agencies reported that they were currently using AI.

Data quality and comprehensive tracking remain unresolved obstacles to government-wide AI governance. The GAO found that five agencies provided comprehensive information for each of their reported AI use cases while the other fifteen had instances of incomplete and inaccurate data. Some inventories did not include required data elements, such as the AI life cycle stage or an indication of whether an AI use case was releasable or not. Two inventories included AI uses that were later determined by the agencies to not be AI. Without accurate inventories, the government's management of its use of AI will be hindered by incomplete and inaccurate data.

Federal compliance with AI policy requirements remains partial and uneven across the government. Ten of twenty-three agencies implemented all AI requirements specific to their agencies, twelve implemented some but not all, and one was exempt from the requirements. The GAO identified that Commerce and the General Services Administration fully implemented selected requirements, with Commerce creating a plan to develop AI technical standards and GSA establishing the AI Center of Excellence. By contrast, the Offices of Management and Budget and Personnel Management did not fully implement selected requirements; OMB has not yet developed guidance for the acquisition and use of AI, and OPM has not yet established or updated an occupational category for those employees performing AI work.

The federal government's investment and policy infrastructure for AI reflects both commitment and structural gaps. The President's fiscal year 2023 budget request included $1.8 billion for nondefense research and development investment in AI. Some agencies are using AI operationally to identify information security threats and facilitate the review of large datasets. However, there is no government-wide guidance on how agencies should acquire and use AI, and federal law and guidance have several requirements for agencies implementing AI that they haven't all been met. Without such guidance, agencies cannot consistently manage AI or effectively address AI risks and benefits.

The international policy landscape shows the OECD and peer organizations developing frameworks for trustworthy AI deployment. The OECD Artificial Intelligence Policy Observatory provides access to 900+ national AI policies and initiatives and works to help AI actors develop and use trustworthy AI systems that respect human rights and are fair, transparent, explainable, robust, secure and safe. In July 2024, the GPAI initiative and OECD member countries' work on AI joined forces under the GPAI brand to create an integrated partnership. Oxford Insights helps governments increase the impact of their public services through empowering teams and harnessing technology, signaling that government AI adoption is framed around service delivery improvements rather than operational efficiency alone.

Regulatory attention to AI is accelerating at the state and federal level. As of the tracking documented here, 4,344 AI bills are tracked across 53 jurisdictions and updated daily. This legislative activity reflects growing recognition that AI deployment in government requires legal frameworks, though the varied pace and substance of bills across states suggests no consensus yet on the rules governing government AI systems. Until requirements for transparent AI inventories, consistent acquisition guidance, and workforce planning are met across federal agencies, the sector will remain fragmented in its capacity to manage both the operational benefits and the documented risks that AI poses.
